questions.q: What is the primary latency benefit of a CDN?
options: Content is served from edge locations near users, shortening the network path
Edge servers use faster CPUs than origin servers, speeding response generation
Requests skip DNS resolution entirely when a CDN sits in front
TCP is replaced by a proprietary protocol that needs no handshake

questions.q: What happens on a CDN cache miss?
options: The edge returns 404 until an operator manually seeds the object
The user's browser is redirected to fetch the object directly from the origin data center
The edge fetches it from the origin or a parent tier, serves it, and caches it
The request is queued at the edge until a scheduled origin sync runs

questions.q: What does a TTL on a cached object control?
options: How many edge locations are allowed to hold a copy of the object
How many client requests the edge may serve before it must revalidate each client
The maximum size of the object the edge is willing to cache
How long the edge may serve the copy before revalidating or refetching

questions.q: What is a cache key?
options: The TLS session ticket used to resume connections at the edge
The set of request attributes (URL, chosen headers) identifying a cached variant
A signed authorization token proving the client is permitted to read the cached object
The origin's private identifier for each file on its local disk

questions.q: Which content is the most natural fit for CDN edge caching?
options: Per-user account dashboards rendered from live database queries
POST endpoints that create new orders in the checkout flow
Static assets such as images, scripts, and video segments
Responses that differ on every request due to random tokens

questions.q: What does cache invalidation (a purge) actually do?
options: Removes or marks stale copies at edges so the next request refetches from origin
Deletes the object from the origin server and every backup simultaneously
Rewrites the object's URL so old links stop resolving at the edge
Forces every client browser worldwide to clear its local copy of the object immediately

questions.q: Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 tells the CDN what?
options: The object must be revalidated against the origin on every single request it receives
Shared caches may store the object and serve it for a day without revalidating
Only the user's private browser cache may store the object for a day
The object may be cached forever because it is immutable content

questions.q: How are users typically routed to a nearby CDN edge?
options: Every edge shares one TCP endpoint and forwards excess users randomly
The origin measures each user's latency and redirects them with an HTTP 302
Clients download a list of edges and ping each one before every request
DNS resolution or anycast steers the client to a close healthy edge

questions.q: What problem does an origin shield (parent cache tier) solve?
options: It encrypts origin traffic that edge locations would otherwise send in plaintext
It load balances user traffic across edge locations during regional failures
It stores objects too large for edge SSDs on cheaper spinning disks
It collapses misses from many edges so the origin sees far fewer requests

questions.q: You configure the cache key to vary on the entire Cookie header. What is the consequence?
options: Responses get cached once and then served to the wrong logged-in users
Hit rate collapses because nearly every user produces a distinct variant
The CDN refuses to cache anything carrying cookies and returns errors
Cookies get stripped from forwarded requests, silently logging users out

questions.q: How do fingerprinted filenames (app.3f9c.js) interact with CDN caching on deploys?
options: New content gets a new URL, so long TTLs are safe and purges are rarely needed
Fingerprints force the CDN to revalidate the bundle on every request
They only work if the TTL is kept shorter than the deploy interval
They require a global purge on each deploy to avoid serving stale code

questions.q: A viral object expires at thousands of edges at once. What protects the origin?
options: Anycast rerouting that spreads the refetches across all origin regions evenly
Client retry budgets that stop browsers from re-requesting stale objects
Request coalescing plus stale-while-revalidate so one refetch serves the crowd
Automatic TTL doubling whenever the origin's error rate starts rising

questions.q: Why is caching authenticated API responses at the edge risky?
options: A shared cache may serve one user's private data to another without careful keying
Authenticated responses are always uncacheable at the HTTP protocol level
Edge caches are technically incapable of storing any response to requests carrying an Authorization header
Tokens expire mid-TTL, which corrupts the cached response body itself

questions.q: Negative caching: why cache 404 responses briefly?
options: To satisfy HTTP specs that require 404s be cached for at least an hour
So clients stop retrying, because cached 404s disable browser retries
To keep bots from discovering which URLs actually exist at the origin
To stop repeated misses for missing objects from hammering the origin

questions.q: Why do HLS/DASH video segments cache so well on CDNs?
options: Video codecs include CDN hints that force every edge to prefetch them
Players re-request the manifest, which pins all segments into edge memory
Segments are small immutable files shared by every viewer of that stream
Segment URLs rotate every few seconds, keeping caches perpetually warm

questions.q: You set s-maxage=600 and max-age=60. How do the CDN and browser behave?
options: Both caches use 600 seconds because the larger directive always wins
The CDN serves it for 600 seconds; browsers revalidate after 60
The browser serves it for 600 seconds; the CDN revalidates after 60
The directives conflict, so both caches revalidate on every request

questions.q: Purge-on-change vs short TTLs for a breaking-news site: what is the tradeoff?
options: Purges are free while short TTLs raise CDN bills, so purging always wins
Short TTLs bound staleness but raise origin load; purges are precise but harder to operate
Short TTLs cannot go below one hour, so purging is the only real option
Purging additionally clears every client browser's cache, while TTLs only ever affect the edge tier

questions.q: After adding a random analytics query param to asset URLs, origin load spikes despite long TTLs. Why?
options: Random params make responses larger, so the origin needs more bandwidth
The CDN treats requests with random params as POSTs, which are never cached
Each unique URL is a distinct cache key, so most requests now miss
TTLs reset whenever the query string changes, expiring existing objects

questions.q: 10M users each fetch a 2 MB bundle daily; the CDN hit rate is 90%. Approximate daily origin egress for it?
options: About 20 TB, since every request ultimately originates at the origin
Roughly 20 GB, since only manifest requests ever reach the origin
Roughly 18 TB, which is the share of traffic the edge absorbs
About 2 TB, the 10% of the 20 TB total that misses the edge

questions.q: One PoP serves a corrupted copy of an immutable JS asset after a disk fault. Best remediation lever?
options: Purge the object so that PoP refetches a clean copy from origin or shield
Lower global TTLs so every PoP refreshes the asset more frequently
Fail the entire PoP out of DNS until its disk has been replaced
Re-deploy the application so all asset fingerprints change everywhere
